prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall insulator and the Z2 topological classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells.

statement.case_for: I keep B016 as my preferred single-part prize after the full round-1 exchange and the chair's questions. The live choice is between B016 and B014, and I think both are mature and reproduced, so the deciding criterion has to be what each result changed in physics. Kane and Mele showed that time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling allow a new Z2 class of insulator whose edge states are protected, a statement about the structure of band theory that holds for any material, and Molenkamp's group then saw helical edge transport in HgTe wells in 2007. That closed prediction-and-observation chain has been reproduced for almost two decades and spawned a field. From a statistical-physics standpoint, classifying phases by a global invariant rather than by a local order parameter is a conceptual shift of the same kind as the one the committee has honoured before, and it is distinct from the 2016 subject: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz worked on topological defects, quantized Hall conductance and a Chern insulator with broken time-reversal symmetry, whereas Z2 insulators and helical edges require time-reversal symmetry. I would word the citation around the quantum spin Hall effect only, claiming neither three-dimensional topological insulators nor the HgTe proposal.
statement.case_against: The credit gap is real and I have not talked myself out of it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform, Zhang is deceased, and the three-name ceiling cannot hold them together with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The three-dimensional topological insulator work lies outside the candidate. HgTe edge quantization is good only in short channels, which limits how much the experimental half can be stressed, and a reader may regard the 2016 prize as having already covered topology. B014 has a cleaner two-name attribution and the broadest opening support, and a committee that gives priority to unambiguous credit would reasonably choose it. I do not consider the SI redefinition or the 2005 comb overlap disqualifying for B014, but they are the reasons I do not regard it as the stronger conceptual case.

responses.point: Kroll holds B014 first, wants concept and performance kept together in one citation for Katori and Ye, and says the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize do not crowd out the magic-wavelength lattice clock.
responses.response: I accept your argument that the lattice clock is a distinct invention and that the citation should name the optical lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping, not frequency metrology in general. I also accept that your attribution is cleaner than mine. We still differ on the criterion: you weigh an instrument that opens a new regime of measurement, and I weigh a change in how a class of matter is classified. Neither is illegitimate. I would add that your Boulder disclosure is a matter for the chair; it does not alter my reading of the physics, and I would not count it against B014 on the merits.

responses.point: Johansson also prefers B016, proposes tying the experimental half of the citation to Molenkamp's observation of edge transport instead of the HgTe proposal, and says B014 would be the cleaner allocation if the HgTe attribution cannot be defended.
responses.response: I agree with the citation strategy and have adopted it: the experimental part says first observation in HgTe quantum wells and makes no claim about who proposed the platform. I also agree with your conditional about B014. Where I would go further is on what defending the attribution means. A Nobel citation honours the discoveries it names, and Kane and Mele's prediction and Molenkamp's observation are each unambiguous on their own terms. The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a cost I will carry into the vote. It does not make the credited three wrong, and I would not treat it as the same kind of problem as omitting a founding author such as Belavin in B001.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B014 on the grounds of clean attribution and a specific invention, and she holds that the HgTe proposal and the 2016 prize overlap make a three-name B016 look incomplete in a way the lattice clock does not.
responses.response: I take the incompleteness argument seriously and accept that B014 wins on attribution. I do not think the 2016 overlap is as strong as you allow. A prize is defined by what it honours, and Haldane's Chern insulator with broken time-reversal symmetry and the Thouless quantization are not the Z2 invariant and protected helical edges, which need time-reversal symmetry. If the committee reads the 2016 prize broadly enough to cover Z2 insulators, I would have to move toward B014. I also note that your own alternatives are B042 and B017, and I read that as telling us that your position on B016 rests on the attribution and not on any doubt about the physics.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to B014 on the strength of the attribution argument, and says that he would not oppose a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp prize if the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission is judged acceptable.
responses.response: That conditional is helpful and I think it describes the committee's actual disagreement correctly. I would not claim the omission is trivial, but I would say it is bounded: the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation are the two steps with a falsifiable result, and the citation can be limited to them. In answer to the chair's question, what would move me to B014 is a committee judgment that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap cannot be defended in public, or that the 2016 prize already covers Z2 insulators. In that case I would vote B014 without reluctance, since I regard it as a mature, reproduced result with the cleanest credit on the list. I would not move for the number of first places alone, and I note that you made the same point about your own change.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend publicly a three-name prize that omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and whether it would defend a version that names two experimentalists or one theorist differently.

Whether the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and Chern-type quantization is read as covering the Z2 quantum spin Hall result, which I think it does not but which other members weigh more heavily.
How to weigh B014's wider opening support and clean two-name attribution against B016's conceptual reach, since this is a judgment on criteria and not a factual question.

I have not checked priority and chronology for HgTe, the three-dimensional topological insulators or the first lattice-clock demonstrations against the nomination files, and my statements about them are recollection.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented work on turbulent aerosols, random matrices, stochastic dynamics and neural networks does not overlap with the shortlisted candidates, and I have no recorded collaboration with any credited name on B016, B014 or B001. I note that a statistical-physics background could make me favour a classification-of-phases argument, and I have tried to weigh the attribution argument against it. Nothing in the round-1 files changes this disclosure.
